title: The Thing Keeping Me Safe Was the Thing I Should Have Feared
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis recounts a Sunday-morning email from a senior executive, in the middle of a brutal negotiation she alone could close, that showed her how circumstantial her organizational value really was. When she calmly offered to hand the deal to someone else, he phoned within seconds to soften his message, and she realized the call was about the deal, not about her. She connects that moment to the fear she felt before first publishing her honest writing about work, a fear that presented itself as pragmatism, patience, and providing for her family. Her central claim is that the fear that keeps you small does not feel like fear but like good judgment, and that it feels physically identical to the fear that warns you off a real cliff. She left over a two-year plan, learned to treat fear as information to interpret rather than a verdict, and now asks which kind of scary she is facing. The piece is a first-person case for examining whether your caution protects your life or only your cage.
points: The author argues that a leader's value tied to an unfinished deal is real but circumstantial, and can be spent or recalled by others the moment the work closes.
Her calm, no-heat offer to hand the problem back, while still taking full ownership, revealed how much leverage the executive's pressure actually carried.
Fear that protects the status quo disguises itself as responsible values such as pragmatism, patience, and providing for family, which makes it hard to challenge.
Fear that warns of a real cliff and fear that keeps you small feel the same in the body, so the useful question is which kind it is rather than whether it is scary.
She reframes the 'safe' choice of staying as the one choice guaranteed to deliver the outcome she feared most, a life where her worth was never her own.
quotes: The fear that keeps you where you are does not arrive as fear. It arrives as good judgment.

My value was real, but it was circumstantial. It could be spent, managed, and emailed about on a Sunday, and the moment the deal was signed, it would reset to whatever the next unfinished thing required of me.
It came disguised as every value I respect. Pragmatism. Patience. Providing for my family.

It feels identical, in the body, to the fear that warns you off a genuine cliff. Same churn, same tightening, same airtight case for not moving. One is protecting your life. The other is protecting your cage.
What changed was not the fear. It was how I read it. I stopped treating it as a verdict and started treating it as information to interpret.
The strangest part is that frightening and free turn out to be the same feeling from the inside. The drop in your stomach when you step off the ladder is almost identical to the drop of falling.
I used to be afraid of not climbing high enough. That fear is gone. What scares me now is reaching eighty and not being able to say, in one clear sentence, how my life made something better.
